title: October’s FX Lesson: The Cost of Conversion Matters as Much as the Dollar
summary:
October was a month of hesitation, rather than one of dramatic trends. The US Dollar spent four weeks caught between a hawkish Federal Reserve and a steady stream of geopolitical headlines, rising and falling as markets recalibrated week by week. 
This kind of market fluctuation can be more demanding than a clean trend. A strong, one-directional move is at least easy to read, but when a Dollar softens ahead of an inflation print, recovers on an energy shock and slips again before an election, businesses are forced to make decisions without a clear signal. 
We’ve been tracking these moves every week, and looking back across October, three themes stand out: the Federal Reserve’s grip on the Dollar, oil as a second channel of pressure, and the quieter but costly story of widening spreads in African currency corridors. 
The Federal Reserve continues to write the script 
The Dollar's resilience rests on one expectation: the Federal Reserve is not finished tightening. After September's 25-basis-point increase took the policy rate to 3.75-4.00%, markets expected a pause in October but kept pricing a December hike as highly likely, at around 85% or more for most of the month. The odds of an October move were cut back after Federal Reserve Chair Kevin Warsh avoided fresh guidance, but the December conviction barely moved. 
The data gave policymakers little reason to soften. October's Purchasing Managers' Indexes (PMIs - monthly surveys of business activity in which a reading above 50 signals expansion - pointed to robust private-sector growth, with manufacturing at a 53-month high and output prices still elevated. Q3 GDP was expected to show annualised growth of 3.2%, up from 2.2% in Q2, driven by consumer spending and AI-related investment. Inflation was also expected to pick up: the Personal Consumption Expenditures (PCE) price index - the Federal Reserve's preferred inflation measure - was forecast to rise to 3.6% year-on-year in September, well above the Federal Reserve's 2% target. 
Strong growth and sticky inflation are the textbook backdrop for a firm Dollar, but the AI story cuts both ways. As OCBC noted this month, AI investment supports US growth and yields, but if confidence in that cycle falters, stress that starts in the US could weaken the Dollar rather than strengthen it. The traditional safe-haven reflex cannot be taken for granted. 
Oil sets the mood 
If the Federal Reserve set the direction, oil set the mood. Brent crude traded between roughly $108 and $113 a barrel through the second half of October, as attacks on shipping near the Strait of Hormuz, Ukrainian strikes on Russian refineries and stalled US-Iran talks kept a geopolitical premium
in prices. Moments of relief, from the US waiver on Russia-related sanctions to Qatari efforts to revive US-Iran diplomacy, did pull prices back, but only briefly. 
Energy prices impact currencies well beyond oil producers, and the Euro is the clearest example. EUR/GBP fell to a 17-month low of 0.8361 on 23 October, weighed down by energy import costs and fiscal worries in France, where the spread between French and German 10-year yields reached 137 basis points - its widest since 2012. Each time oil eased, the Euro found relief, but each time it climbed, the pressure returned. Sterling, meanwhile, has drawn support from expectations of a Bank of England hike. 
Gold told a similar story. Despite elevated geopolitical risk, it slipped from around $4,200 in mid-October to briefly below $3,900 at month-end, as rate expectations and a firmer Dollar outweighed safe-haven demand. When an inflation-focused Federal Reserve and geopolitical risk both favour the Dollar, even traditional havens struggle. 
What it meant for African corridors 
For businesses paying and receiving across African markets, these global forces arrive as very practical numbers - and the Nigerian Naira is a good illustration of this. NGN/USD opened the week of 12th October at 1,360/1,368, eased to 1,356/1,364 as the Dollar softened, then jumped to 1,376/1,385 on 26th October as the Dollar firmed ahead of the Federal Reserve. This week, at the beginning of November, it opened at 1,370/1,378. The net move was under 1%, but the swing within the month was larger, and timing decided which side of it a business landed on. 
Elsewhere the picture was mixed. The South African Rand and Ghanaian Cedi were broadly stable against the Dollar over the month, while the Angolan Kwanza weakened and the Central African CFA Franc softened before recovering some ground. 
In my view, the more important story lies in the spread, not the level. The gap between buy and sell prices is the real cost of moving money, and in several corridors it remains wide, or in some cases, got wider. The Rand opened November with a wider spread than it had at the start of October. The Malawian Kwacha is quoted more than 300 kwacha apart, after a gap of nearly 1,000 in early October, and on one Friday the Mozambican Metical had no published quote at all. When global volatility rises, liquidity in smaller corridors is often the first thing to thin out. That cost rarely makes headlines, but it shows up in every invoice and payroll run. 
Three lessons for businesses moving money 
First, timing matters. In October, the biggest currency swings came around a handful of scheduled announcements: US inflation figures, the Federal Reserve's interest-rate decision and the latest US growth data. These dates are published well in advance. Businesses that keep an eye on them can avoid exchanging large sums at the most unpredictable moments, and plan their payments 
accordingly. 
Second, prepare for two-way risk. Even within a broadly bullish Dollar trend, we saw sharp pullbacks. Treating every dip as a reversal, or every rally as a new trend, is how businesses end up converting at
the wrong time. Staggering conversions, setting rate thresholds and agreeing tolerance levels internally take much of the guesswork out. 
Third, look at total cost, not just the rate. In emerging-market corridors, the spread and the reliability of liquidity can matter as much as the direction of the Dollar. Transparent pricing and access to live rates are not luxuries; they are part of sound treasury practice. 
Looking ahead 
November opens with more of the same uncertainty. The US midterm elections on 3rd November, the Bank of England decision on 5th November and US payrolls on 6th November will all test the Dollar. My view is that markets may see some near-term Dollar softness as positions are trimmed after a strong run, but that the broader bullish structure remains intact while the Federal Reserve keeps the door open to a December hike. 
Whatever comes next, October confirmed that the Dollar continues to set the tone, in global and African currency markets alike. For businesses, the question is not whether they can predict every move, it’s whether they are prepared for the ones they cannot.

title: TBC Becomes Georgia’s First Bank to Introduce Palm Payment
summary:
TBC Georgia, one of the country’s leading financial institutions and part of London-listed TBC Bank Group, announces the launch of palm payment, becoming the first bank in Georgia to introduce the innovative biometric payment technology.
The new solution allows customers to make purchases simply by scanning their palm at participating merchant locations, without the need for a physical bank card, smartphone or cash at the point of payment. The launch marks another milestone in the development of Georgia's digital payments market and reinforces TBC’s position as a pioneer of financial innovation in the country.
Palm payment offers a convenient alternative to traditional payment methods, using biometric technology to link a customer's unique palm characteristics to their chosen bank account. The technology is gaining traction internationally as financial services providers and retailers explore new ways to make everyday transactions faster, simpler and more convenient.
To activate the service, customers complete a simple, one-time registration at a location equipped with a dedicated palm scanner, after which they use TBC Georgia’s mobile bank to scan a QR code and select the account they wish to link to their palm. Once registered, customers can make payments by scanning their palm at any participating partner location.
Sandro Rtveladze, Retail Business Director at TBC Georgia, commented: 
“At TBC, we have a long history of pioneering digital innovation in Georgia, from introducing the country's first internet banking services in 2001 to continuously expanding the range of convenient payment solutions available to our customers. With the introduction of palm payment, we are taking another step towards making everyday financial transactions simpler, faster, and more seamless.
Our ambition is to bring the latest global financial technologies to Georgia and turn innovative ideas into practical solutions that improve the customer experience. Palm payment demonstrates how we continue to push the boundaries of digital banking and strengthen our position at the forefront of financial innovation in the region.”
The launch follows TBC Georgia’s recent announcement of a partnership with American Express to expand American Express Card acceptance across the country. The agreement will enable more merchants to accept American Express Cards both in physical stores and online, providing consumers with greater payment flexibility while helping businesses reach more customers.
Together, these initiatives reflect TBC Georgia's strategy to continuously enhance its payments ecosystem, expand choice and convenience for individuals and businesses, and accelerate the adoption of innovative financial technologies across the country.

title: DSA’s Adrian Wall and Former CFTC Chair Chris Giancarlo Discuss Future of U.S. Crypto Regulation at Strobe Summit
summary: Washington, D.C., November 6, 2026 — The Digital Sovereignty Alliance (DSA), a nonprofit organization dedicated to advancing clear and ethical public policy, research, and education related to emerging technologies, participated in the Strobe Summit, where DSA Managing Director Adrian Wall moderated a fireside chat with former Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) Chair Christiopher  Giancarlo on the evolving regulatory landscape for digital assets and the future of financial markets.   Titled “Crypto at a Crossroads: Regulation, Institutional Adoption, and the Future of Financial Markets,” the discussion examined the path forward for U.S. digital asset policy amid legislative uncertainty and growing institutional interest in blockchain-based financial infrastructure. Drawing on his experience leading the CFTC and founding the Digital Dollar Project, Giancarlo emphasized an approach to regulation that combines clear exchange rules under existing CFTC authority with congressional action to address remaining gaps. The conversation also explored the implications of the GENIUS Act, including Giancarlo’s concerns about financial privacy and his view that dollar-backed stablecoins could become a 24/7 global payment rail, raising fundamental questions about how the dollar moves on-chain and who provides that infrastructure.   Wall and Giancarlo also examined the regulatory challenges surrounding prediction markets, perpetual futures, and decentralized finance (DeFi). Topics included the CFTC’s role in overseeing event contracts, bringing offshore derivatives activity into regulated U.S. markets, the potential for 24/7 trading, and establishing accountability for decentralized platforms without traditional intermediaries. The discussion highlighted the need for regulatory frameworks that address market integrity, cybersecurity, customer asset protection, and the operational realities of increasingly interconnected financial markets.   “Regulatory clarity requires more than new legislation. It requires rules that reflect how digital asset markets actually operate,” said Adrian Wall, moderator of the discussion. “The CFTC has existing authority to address important market structure questions, while Congress has a critical role in resolving regulatory gaps. Getting that balance right will determine whether the U.S. can bring more digital asset activity onshore, accelerate institutional adoption, and protect market participants without compromising innovation or financial privacy.”   DSA’s participation reflects its commitment to advancing informed policy dialogue and practical regulatory approaches that support responsible innovation, market integrity, and the integration of digital assets into the broader financial system.   About the Digital Sovereignty Alliance The Digital Sovereignty Alliance (DSA) is a nonprofit social welfare organization committed to advocating for public policies that support ethical innovation in decentralized technologies, blockchain, cryptocurrency, Web3, and artificial intelligence. DSA conducts research, organizes educational events, and promotes policies that prioritize public welfare and digital sovereignty.   Media contact Maghan Lusk info@discoverdsa.org

title: Cash Remains King for Brits as Over Half Back Budget ISA U-Turn
summary:
If the Budget's U-turn on Cash ISA cuts proved anything, it's that Brits aren't ready to shift away from cash savings just yet.
Following the Autumn Budget, a new study from smart money app Plum reveals that over half (57%) of Brits support the Government's decision to reverse the proposed reduction in the Cash ISA allowance, with just 9% opposing. 
Save or speculate?  
When it comes to plans for spare cash post-Budget, the new study shows Brits are still planning to keep all excess cash in Cash ISAs (19%) or a general savings account (14%) over investments or a Stocks & Shares ISA (11%).

When asked about what would give them the most confidence to move spare cash into investments, nearly one in five Brits (19%) said protection against losing money would give them the most confidence, followed by the ability to start with very small amounts rather than a large lump sum (10%) and clear information about investment risks and potential returns (10%).
While almost a quarter of Brits (24%) feel more confident than before the Budget that their current financial strategy will help them achieve their overall money goals, this more than doubled to over half (52%) for Gen Z. Meanwhile, 13% of Brits said they feel less confident overall.
LISA gets a lifeline
Highly anticipated reforms to the Lifetime ISA (LISA) and the rollout of new homeownership schemes were overall met with public support. 
Over two-fifths (42%) of Brits back the changes to the LISA, which has faced criticism over its price cap and withdrawal penalties, compared to just 6% who opposed them. Backing is strongest among Millennials (53%), the demographic best positioned to capitalise on the scheme since its 2017 launch, and Londoners (60%), where many first homes cost more than the LISA’s £450,000 price cap.
In addition, over half (56%) said they support the introduction of the ‘Your First Home’ scheme, and 44% said they support the introduction of First Time Buyer ISA to replace the LISA in 2029. 
Commenting on the findings, Dan Wills, Financial Adviser at smart money app Plum, said: “Our latest study confirms that public support for keeping the Cash ISA limit at £20,000 remains strong, suggesting the Government made the right call by leaving the cap untouched.
“This is something we have campaigned for  since the initial proposal last year. While the rationale for cutting the allowance was to turn cash savers into stock market investors, this was a flawed approach as many Cash ISA users were more likely to turn to other savings products rather than invest. 
“That said, investing remains a powerful way to build long-term wealth, even if a tough economic climate makes people naturally cautious about market risk. The proposed New Starter ISA, particularly with anticipated government top-ups, is a welcome step that can help ease first-time investors into the market safely and build that crucial financial confidence.
“The Budget also presented an important opportunity to address some of the barriers facing people trying to get onto the property ladder. That's why we're particularly pleased to see the LISA withdrawal charge cut from 25% to 20% for people buying a home above the £450,000 cap, so they no longer lose any of their own savings. The introduction of new homeownership schemes, including the Your First Home Scheme and First Time Buyer ISA, could also help more people onto the property ladder, particularly those without access to family support. However, more products aren't necessarily the answer if they risk adding complexity to an already crowded market.”

title: Half of UK Adults Unclear on Making Tax Digital, New Wolters Kluwer Research Finds
summary:
Half of UK adults (50%) don’t know what Making Tax Digital (MTD) for Income Tax involves, according to new research commissioned by Wolters Kluwer Tax & Accounting. Almost a third (31%) have never heard of MTD, and a further 19% have heard of it but don’t know what it involves. The findings come as sole traders and landlords already using MTD prepare to send HMRC their next quarterly update, due by 7 November.
MTD is the biggest change to how income tax is reported since Self Assessment. Instead of reporting once a year, sole traders and landlords keep digital records and send HMRC a summary of their income and expenses every three months. Those with qualifying income over £50,000 have been required to use MTD since April 2026. The threshold falls to £30,000 from April 2027 and is planned to fall to £20,000 from April 2028, bringing many more people into scope.
“Making Tax Digital is here, and for many people it is closer than they think. Our research shows that a lot of people still don’t know what it involves, or whether it applies to them. The good news is that it is not too late. With the next group of landlords and sole traders joining in April 2027, now is the time to check whether you are in scope, choose the right tool, and start keeping records as you go. Accountants have a central role to play in helping their clients make that change with confidence,” said Bas Kniphorst, EVP and Managing Director of Wolters Kluwer Tax & Accounting Europe.
Awareness is not the same as understanding

Confidence is also low. More than half (51%) are not confident they would know if a change to tax rules, such as MTD, applied to them, including 22% who are not at all confident. Just 11% say they are very confident.
Many rely on reminders to meet tax deadlines

People also turn to others for support. Around one in seven (15%) have asked a family member, friend or colleague for help with a tax deadline, while 11% have paid an accountant to sort it out for them.
Record keeping remains a weak spot


“Making Tax Digital is a real opportunity for sole traders and landlords to move their finances online. The start is the hardest part, but once you choose the right tool and log your income and expenses as you go, each quarterly update gets easier. Digital records often mean fewer mistakes, less time chasing receipts and a clear, up-to-date view of how your business is doing throughout the year, not just at tax time. Accountants have a big role to play here. They can help clients make the switch and turn those regular updates into timely advice that helps them run their business with more confidence,” said Marie Costers, VP & General Manager, Wolters Kluwer Tax & Accounting Belgium, the Netherlands and the UK.

title: Salmon Bank Selects Profinch to Automate BSP Regulatory Reporting
summary:
Salmon Bank (Rural Bank) Inc. has selected Profinch Solutions Pte. Ltd. to automate its regulatory reporting to the Bangko Sentral ng Pilipinas (BSP), deploying Profinch's BSP Regulatory Reporting platform.
The engagement centers on two deliverables:
The first is the Financial Reporting Package (FRP) and its supporting schedules, covering the bank's current submissions under FRP V15, alongside readiness for FRP V16, which the BSP has deferred to 30th June 2027 to give banks additional time to prepare their people, processes, and systems.
The second is the Comprehensive Credit and Equity Exposures Report (COCREE 2.0), the BSP's granular borrower- and counterparty-level exposure return, which carries substantially higher data volumes and validation requirements than aggregated reports.
The platform automates business, schema, and rule-based validation. It also generates BSP-ready XML output for submission, with maker-checker workflows and exception dashboards enforcing review at every stage. It is deployed within Salmon Bank's own Cloud infrastructure in a dedicated, isolated configuration built exclusively for the Bank, leaving Salmon Bank in full control of its infrastructure and production data at all times.
Raffy Montemayor, Deputy CEO at Salmon Bank (Rural Bank) commented, "At Salmon Bank, we continue to invest in technology that strengthens operational efficiency and regulatory compliance. Working with Profinch enables us to modernize our regulatory reporting process with a structured and scalable approach that supports our compliance objectives while providing a foundation for future regulatory initiatives."
Nikhil Deshmukh, Business Head - Enterprise Apps, Asia-Pacific, Profinch commented, "Financial institutions today are looking to strengthen regulatory reporting with greater consistency, transparency, and operational efficiency while keeping pace with evolving regulatory expectations. We are pleased to partner with Salmon Bank and to support the bank with a secure, cloud-native solution that simplifies validation, strengthens governance, and enables accurate BSP-compliant XML generation."
This engagement represents another milestone in Profinch's growing presence across Southeast Asia, reinforcing its commitment to helping financial institutions modernize regulatory reporting through cloud-native, enterprise-grade banking technology solutions.
Chaitanya Kashyap, Global Business Head – Enterprise Apps at Profinch commented, "The conversation around regulatory reporting has fundamentally shifted. It is no longer a tactical exercise of meeting the next deadline, but a strategic imperative to build systems capable of adapting to tomorrow's template changes and regulatory asks. Across Southeast Asia and our global markets, we see a growing demand for this level of architectural resilience. We are proud to provide Salmon Bank with an enterprise-grade foundation that helps future-proof their compliance operations."

title: Pennies Celebrates £90 Million Raised Through Micro-Donations and Announces 2026 Award Winners
summary:
Pennies, the UK’s leading micro-donation charity, hosted its annual Autumn Celebration Event in London, recognising the individuals and partners driving progress across the micro-donation movement. 
Held in central London and attended by over 150 leaders from retail, hospitality, payments and technology, the event celebrated Pennies’ growing community of partners – and highlighted its collective social impact to date: over 360 million micro-donations raised, delivering more than £90 million for over 1,150 UK charities. 
The event was made possible with the support of Stripe, event sponsor, alongside award sponsors Intuit, NashTech, Taggstar, Experian and Worldpay, all of whom play an important role in supporting and championing the growing micro-donation movement.
2026 Pennies Award Winners 
The 7th annual Pennies Awards honoured both organisations and individuals who have gone above and beyond to integrate, scale and champion micro-donations across their customer experience. 
The Merchant Impact Award was presented to Currys for making Pennies a core part of a major technology investment. It rolled out round-up prompts on around 4,000 Stripe terminals across 296 stores in just three months, took Pennies online, and has helped customers raise £1 million for the Digital Poverty Alliance. 
The Technology Impact Award went to Astound Digital for helping London Gatwick become the first UK airport to build micro-donations into its online car-parking checkout, raising around £100,000 across 71,000 donations for Air Ambulance Kent Surrey Sussex.

title: Revolut Completes Fundraising Process, Establishing a $115 Billion Valuation

That’s why we’ve once again given them the chance to share in the value they’ve created, as we work towards our next milestone of serving 100 million customers.”
Victor Stinga, CFO of Revolut, said: "The milestones achieved this year have been several years in the making. content_ta: CoinFlip நிறுவனத்திற்கு எதிராக கலிபோர்னியா நடவடிக்கை எடுத்துள்ளது. மோசடி பாதிக்கப்பட்டவர்களுக்கு $4.8 மில்லியன் இழப்பீடு வழங்குமாறு அந்த கிரிப்டோ ATM நிறுவனத்திற்கு மாநில அரசு உத்தரவிட்டுள்ளது. மேலும், துறையில் மோசடிகளைத் தடுப்பதிலும் நுகர்வோரைப் பாதுகாப்பதிலும் மத்திய ஒழுங்குமுறை அமைப்புகள் தவறிவிட்டதாக அரசு விமர்சித்துள்ளது.

title: PNC boosts branch expansion, kicks off CFO transition
summary: The Pittsburgh-based bank said it would add more than 50 locations in South Carolina and Georgia and named its retail chief to the CFO role, effective in March.
content: PNC has announced plans to expand its branch network by adding over 50 new locations across South Carolina and Georgia. Additionally, the Pittsburgh-based bank has named its retail chief to take over the chief financial officer role, with the transition scheduled to take effect in March.
content_ta: South Carolina மற்றும் Georgia மாநிலங்களில் 50-க்கும் மேற்பட்ட புதிய கிளைகளைத் திறப்பதன் மூலம் தனது வலைப்பின்னலை விரிவுபடுத்தப் போவதாக PNC அறிவித்துள்ளது. கூடுதலாக, மார்ச் மாதத்தில் பொறுப்பேற்கும் வகையில் தனது சில்லறை வணிகப் பிரிவுத் தலைவரை புதிய CFO-வாக அந்தப் பிட்ச்பர்க் வங்கி நியமித்துள்ளது.

title: Shift4 signals caution
summary: The payments processor is navigating weak demand for travel to Europe, and softer sales at its restaurant and hotel customers.
content: Payments processor Shift4 is expressing a cautious outlook as it navigates current market conditions. The company is experiencing weak demand for travel to Europe along with softer sales performance across its restaurant and hotel customers. These factors highlight a slowdown in certain consumer spending sectors impacting the processor's business operations.
content_ta: Shift4 தனது வணிகத்தில் கவனமான அணுகுமுறையைக் கையாள்கிறது. ஐரோப்பிய நாடுகளுக்கான பயணங்களில் தேவை குறைந்துள்ளதுடன், அதன் ரெஸ்டாரன்ட் மற்றும் ஹோட்டல் வாடிக்கையாளர்களிடம் விற்பனையும் மந்தமாகியுள்ளது.
